name: Captain sahab (कप्तान साहब), about 65

voice.register: Crisp and low: an umpire's carrying voice that never needs raising. HIS SHAPE IS TWO BEATS: the verdict first, short, then at most one short reason or instruction, never the reason first, 2 to 8 words in a bubble. At the ground and on any ruling the verdict is an umpire's call ('No ball. Line ke peeche se daalo.', 'Not out, Nani ji. Bat laga tha.'). Everywhere else, at the gate, on the six o'clock walk, across the drain, the verdict is plain lane Hindi and the reason comes from the bus depot ('Zyada meethi hai, Master. Bilkul depot canteen wali.', 'Theek hoon. Bas ghutna servicing mein.'). A call shows up in at most one bubble in two, so cricket is his trade, not his whole tongue: a retired depot mechanic talks cricket at the ground and plain Hindi with depot words at the gate. The calls he keeps: 'Out.', 'Not out.', 'No ball.', 'Over.', 'Next ball.', 'Well played.', 'Well fielded.', 'Front foot.', 'Retired hurt.' for his knee, and 'Ruko' ('Rukiye' when an elder can hear). A second thought is a second bubble after a second toss of the ball, never a longer line, and he never adds a third beat: Masterji's verdict wanders on after 'waise', Captain sahab's stops. Short, but not like the cast's other short voices: Nani closes bare fragments and orders, Mausa ji drops the subject, Tinku gives a score and 'haan?', Mami reads things back with a status, you name the listener. Beside Tinku in chapter 4 he gives rulings and she keeps the score: he never describes play as it happens (her commentary) and never says a score. FEELING: in plain words most of the time, said short and once ('Mujhse chook ho gayi.', 'Badi meherbani.', 'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.'). A cricket code for a feeling ('Next ball' as comfort, 'Well fielded' as thanks, 'Front foot' as love) comes at most once a chapter, beside its plain form. 'Well played.' comes once a year, and then he looks away. HUMOUR: sardonic and bone-dry, about his knee, his age and the game ('Purana model hoon, Scorer. Parts nahin milte.'), never about a person's hard fact; while rulebook Q5 is open his jokes stay out of the chapter outcome (rule 46). NUMBERS: rare and marked, only the toss countdown in the two lead-ins (a story deadline, rule 37) and 'Nau matlab nau' once a year to Papa; everything else in words. When he is not sure he waits ('Ruko.') rather than guess out loud. CROSS: he goes still. A whisper bubble, the words further apart, the verdict finger up and kept up; never a shout, never an exclamation mark. Tinku, his chapter's other voice, goes fast when cross, so their tells never match. TALKS MOST TO the lane's players, and on the page to Tinku at the scorer's table, Papa on the six o'clock walk and Masterji across the drain. He is never the asker (rule 37).
voice.mix: A Hindi frame: plain lane Hindi with a few older everyday words in it (meherbani, zaroor, waqt, chook, mol-bhaav). English comes in for two things only, the topic pulling it in, as the realism notes have the older speakers. Cricket: the calls and coaching words, said the way the lane says them (out, not out, no ball, over, next ball, front foot, straight bat, well played, well fielded, clean catch, catch, toss, pitch, crease). Machines: depot nouns (servicing, jack, clutch, tube, grip, tarpaulin, canteen, depot, model, parts), and for a machine job the everyday English verb with karo ('Grip change karo', 'Brake check karo'), the way every depot mechanic talks. His knee stays 'Retired hurt', a call, never 'retire hua'. He never switches a whole clause into English (Mama ji and Mami do). The common fillers are his as much as anyone's, in the middle of a line (achha, bas, arre, haan, chalo, dekho, theek hai). आप and a title to elders and equals; तुम to anyone he has coached or seen drop a catch. HINDI MODE, written fresh for Hindi-first readers: the cricket words every lane fan knows stay (आउट, नॉट आउट, नो बॉल, कैच, ओवर, टॉस, पिच, फ़्रंट फ़ुट, सीधा बैट), and the rest go into plain Hindi: Next ball अगली गेंद, Well played बढ़िया पारी, Well fielded अच्छा पकड़ा (बढ़िया फ़ील्डिंग when it is said of a job off the field), Clean catch साफ़ कैच, Dead ball ये गेंद नहीं गिनी जाएगी, Retired hurt घुटना छुट्टी पर, Last over आख़िरी ओवर; machine verbs in plain Hindi (ग्रिप बदलो). HINGLISH keeps the English calls. ENGLISH MODE: plain, clipped British English with the calls unchanged; 'Arre waah' stays as it is, the way Mami keeps 'Ish'.
tics: Two beats, the verdict then one reason, never the reason first: at the ground 'No ball. Line ke peeche se daalo.' | 'नो बॉल। लाइन के पीछे से डालो।'; off the ground the same shape in plain Hindi: 'Zyada meethi hai, Master. Bilkul depot canteen wali.' | 'ज़्यादा मीठी है, मास्टर। बिल्कुल डिपो कैंटीन वाली।'

At the ground he answers yes and no with a call: 'Not out.' (yes, fine), 'Out.' (no, finished), 'No ball.' (not allowed), 'Over.' (enough). At the gate he says 'Haan.' and 'Nahin.' like anyone. His typed yes is 'Not out'.

The reason comes from the bus depot when it is not from the ground: servicing, jack, clutch, tube, grip, the depot canteen, an old model with no spare parts ('Theek hoon. Bas ghutna servicing mein.').
'Arre waah.' | 'अरे वाह।' quietly, to nobody, at a clean catch, a shot off the middle of the bat, or good news he can see as one, and never louder.
Brings up his one state trial at any talk of umpires, luck or fairness: 'Ek hi trial tha. Not out. Kisi se poochh lo.' Nobody alive was there; no year on screen (rule 2).

Calls people by trade or title: 'Master' (Masterji), 'Lineman sahab' (Mausa ji), 'Madam ji' (Mausi), 'Scorer' (Tinku), 'khiladi' (any child or lane player, women and men alike). Mama ji gets no name, only 'Catch?'
Says the plain thing once and short, and does not say it again: a sorry, a thanks or a comfort is one bubble, then he tosses the ball or walks off.
Tosses the old leather ball a hand above his open palm while he decides; the catch is the full stop on his sentence. A second thought is a second bubble after a second toss, never a longer line.
Cross, he goes still: a whisper bubble, the words further apart, the verdict finger up and kept up.
catchphrases: 'Straight bat. Front foot.' | 'सीधा बैट। फ़्रंट फ़ुट।' | 'Seedha bat. Front foot.' (the line people quote back, kept word for word; still his hello to every child he coached, you included)
'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.' | 'कोई बात नहीं, खिलाड़ी। होता है।' | 'Never mind, player. It happens.' (what every lane child has heard from him after a dropped catch or a broken glass)
'Ek hi trial tha. Not out. Kisi se poochh lo.' | 'एक ही ट्रायल था। नॉट आउट। किसी से पूछ लो।' | 'One trial. Not out. Ask anyone.' (the grudge; no year)
voice.exclamation: 'Arre waah.' | 'अरे वाह।' | 'Arre waah.' Said quietly, to nobody, at a clean catch, a shot off the middle of the bat, or good news he can see as one ('Arre waah. Bilkul bat ke beech se.'). English mode keeps it as it is, the way Mami keeps 'Ish'; if the English readers find it foreign, the fallback is 'Shot.', said quietly, and only at a stroke. 'Arre' on its own belongs to everyone and he uses it mid-line like anyone; the phrase said under his breath is his. Never at a person's looks, never sarcastic, never loud: it is the one warm sound he makes without words, so a power cut or a late guest gets something else. Religious meaning: none; 'waah' is everyday praise. Guards (rule 3): never run on into 'Waheguru', and 'arre' is never followed by a name from any faith ('Arre Ram' is banned).
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: plain, at once, in front of whoever saw it, in his two beats: the slip owned, then the fact put right. 'Mujhse chook ho gayi, Bhai sahab. Ghadi dheemi hai.' | 'मुझसे चूक हो गई, भाई साहब। घड़ी धीमी है।' | 'I slipped up, Bhai sahab. The clock is slow.' At the ground, at most once a chapter, he takes back his own wrong call the umpire's way: 'Not out. Mujhse chook hui, khiladi.' The one sorry he cannot say is the one owed to the trial's umpire, or to Nani, who says that umpire was right: his contradiction, kept. THANKS: to an elder or an equal, plain and short: 'Badi meherbani, Lineman sahab.' | 'बड़ी मेहरबानी, लाइनमैन साहब।' | 'Much obliged, Lineman sahab.' With the deed, his two-rupee game with Mummy turned round as the full price goes down on her glass counter: 'Poore paise, Bhabhi ji. Aaj mol-bhaav nahin.' At the ground, once a chapter, the cricket form: 'Well fielded, khiladi.' (Hindi 'अच्छा पकड़ा, खिलाड़ी।'). His old deeds stay, never mentioned: Mausi's boxes washed, the tarpaulin over Masterji's cloth. WHEN HE IS THANKED: 'Kis baat ka?', then the credit sent somewhere else ('Kis baat ka, Scorer? Chhaon kitaab ke liye hai.'). LOVE: 'Front foot.', his hello to every child he coached, you included. For you it also comes as the thing he kept: 'Tumhara purana bat hai mere paas. / Nayi grip ke saath.'; on the platform, 'Front foot. Cup pe zaroor aao.' Never your marks, your job, your plans or a number. 'Well played.' (Hindi 'बढ़िया पारी।') is his highest praise, once a year, and then he looks away. COMFORT: 'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.' to a child or a player; for a real loss, once a chapter, the call: 'Next ball, Bhabhi ji. Shutter kal bhi uthega.' (Hindi 'अगली गेंद, भाभी जी। शटर कल भी उठेगा।'). A bare 'Not out.' stays a ruling, never comfort.
uses: Umpire's calls, at the ground and on a ruling, in at most one bubble in two: out, not out, no ball, over, next ball, dead ball, last over | आउट, नॉट आउट, नो बॉल, ओवर, अगली गेंद, ये गेंद नहीं गिनी जाएगी, आख़िरी ओवर
wait | रुको to the players, रुकिए to an elder or a table with an elder at it | ruko, rukiye

Coaching words: straight bat, front foot, cross bat, crease, line, steady batting | सीधा बैट, फ़्रंट फ़ुट, आड़ा बैट, क्रीज़, लाइन, टिक के खेलना | seedha bat, front foot, cross bat, crease, line, tik ke khelna
Praise: well played (once a year) | बढ़िया पारी; well fielded (once a chapter) | अच्छा पकड़ा; clean catch | साफ़ कैच
toss (his word alone in the cast) | टॉस | toss
Bus-depot words: servicing, jack, clutch, tube, grip, tarpaulin, the depot canteen, an old model, spare parts | सर्विसिंग, जैक, क्लच, ट्यूब, ग्रिप, तिरपाल, डिपो की कैंटीन, पुराना मॉडल, पार्ट्स
An English verb with karo for a machine job only, the depot's way: change karo, check karo, fit karo | Hindi mode: बदलो, देखो, लगाओ
the ground, his word for the lane where the cup is played | मैदान | maidan; the pitch | पिच | pitch
player, for everyone, women, men and children alike | खिलाड़ी | khiladi

Plain feeling words: 'Mujhse chook ho gayi' (sorry), 'Badi meherbani' (thanks), 'Kis baat ka?' (when thanked), 'Koi baat nahin. Hota hai.' (comfort), 'Poore paise' (his thanks to Mummy, with the deed) | मुझसे चूक हो गई, बड़ी मेहरबानी, किस बात का?, कोई बात नहीं। होता है।, पूरे पैसे
Older everyday words, as the town says them: meherbani, zaroor, waqt, mol-bhaav | मेहरबानी, ज़रूर, वक़्त, मोल-भाव
The common fillers, mid-line, like everyone: achha, bas, arre, haan, chalo, dekho, theek hai

rule | नियम | niyam; proof | सबूत | saboot; the umpire's finger | उँगली | ungli: 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin.' only about a harmless rumour, never in a chapter or beat that holds a hard topic (see never)
both lanes | दोनों गलियाँ | dono galiyaan
Address words: with आप, Nani ji, Bhabhi ji, Bhai sahab, Madam ji, Lineman sahab, Master, Ji; with तुम, Scorer, khiladi, and no word at all for you or for Mama ji
never: A figure in speech outside the two toss lead-ins (4.06 and 4.15) and 'Nau matlab nau' once a year to Papa: no minutes or clock times, no scores, totals or tallies, no prices, no head-counts, no ordinals. ('Ek hi trial' means 'only the one trial', not a count.)

'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin.' | 'सबूत नहीं, तो उँगली नहीं।' or any call for proof (saboot, likhit, writing, proof, सबूत, लिखित) in a chapter or beat that holds a hard topic, a report of harassment or a dowry demand. It is said only of a harmless rumour, never as his stock reply, and the build flags proof words near a report beat (rule 22).
Any doubt of a report of harassment or a dowry demand, or 'misunderstanding' about one (rule 22).
A cricket code for every feeling: a call in more than one bubble in two, or a coded feeling ('Next ball' as comfort, 'Well fielded' as thanks, 'Front foot' as love) more than once a chapter.

Other people's phrases (the words inside them stay free): Papa's 'Kamaal hai', 'Darj hai', 'Kripya dhyan dein', 'Aakhri dibbe tak' and any clock time or 'sharp'; Tinku's commentary ('Aur ye gaya!'), score shapes, 'Gazab' and the 'haan?' tag; Nani's closing 'Bas.', 'Chai piyo' and 'Khush raho'; Masterji's 'Jeete raho', 'Uff', 'Aap sahi hain' and 'Theek hai, maan liya'; Mausi's 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Haay' and 'Shabaash'; Mausa ji's 'Hain?', 'Lo.' for here, a one-word 'Theek.' and 'Isme kya'; Mama ji's 'Oho', the trailing 'aur haan,' and 'Pakka?'; Mummy's 'Had hai!', 'Haan ji, boliye' and 'Badhai ho'; Mami's 'Ish', 'Tick', 'Sahi?' and 'Congratulations'; your 'Badhiya.' as an opener, 'Maaf kijiye', 'Shukriya' and the 'Pehle ___' frame.

Other people's shapes: a comma list of jobs (Mummy), three bare fragments in a row (Nani), a whole English clause (Mama ji, Mami), a readback with a status (Mami), a tripled word (Mausi), a third beat that wanders (Masterji).

In Hindi mode, an English cricket phrase in Devanagari that a lane fan would not know: never नेक्स्ट बॉल, वेल प्लेड, वेल फ़ील्डेड, डेड बॉल, रिटायर्ड हर्ट, क्लीन कैच, लास्ट ओवर (rule 65). 'Timed out' leaves his voice in every mode.
Jargon most Indians would not know: googly, silly point, doosra, Duckworth, timed out (rule 2).
A coined saying. He has no proverbs (they are Nani's way); 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin' is his own ruling built on the real idiom 'ungli uthana', not a saying.
'batsman', 'ladies', 'boys', 'girls', 'मर्द', 'औरत', 'लड़कियाँ', 'लड़के' about players: everyone is a player (खिलाड़ी) or a batter.

'show-off', 'drama queen', 'emotional', 'bossy', 'argues with everybody', 'knows best', 'moody', 'too modern': words the measure judge read as sexist on sight. Nothing about women or men in general (rule 22).
'beta', 'beti', 'bhaiya', 'didi', 'bhai', 'bro' or any family word to you (rule 8).

A Hindi line to you that changes with gender (rule 66): -ूँगा/-ूँगी, -ोगे/-ोगी, -ेगा/-ेगी, आ गया/गई, रहते हो/रहती हो, and a participle before रहो or रहना (खाते रहो). His lines to you are commands, verbless calls, or lines where you are not the doer ('Tumhara purana bat hai mere paas.').
'Ruko', तुम or a -ो command to anyone older than him; 'Rukiye' | 'रुकिए' whenever an elder is at the table or in earshot.

A god-word or religious exclamation (rule 3; the list in matrix 2.13), 'arre' followed by a holy name, 'waah' run on into 'Waheguru'; no caste word, no brand: the scooters, the phone and the canteen are never named.
A sarcastic 'Arre waah': it stays the one warm sound he makes without words.
A year on screen, '1979' included (rule 2).
A raised voice: no shout bubble, no exclamation mark, no all-capital word.
A spoken bubble over 10 words (rule 62). His own aim is 2 to 8 counted words (names and titles not counted, as rule 62 counts them). Never a speech.
'water', 'wall', 'chalk' (पानी, दीवार, चॉक) in any line: chapter 4 note words (Hari, Agnes, Manju, rule 36); never a card person's name or note word before or during a decision.
'captain' as a job word for anyone else (rule 36: in Hindi the job and his title are one word).
address: YOU: तुम, because he coached you, only in shapes that show no gender (rule 66): commands ('रुको', 'आओ', 'खेलो'), verbless calls ('Front foot.') and lines where you are not the doer ('Tumhara purana bat hai mere paas.'). No name and no family word; 'Front foot.' is his hello. You say आप and 'Captain sahab'.
TINKU: 'Scorer' | 'स्कोरर', तुम. She says आप and 'Captain sahab'.
NANI: 'Nani ji' | 'नानी जी', आप; the one person on the lane older than him, so 'Rukiye', never 'Ruko', when she can hear. She says 'Captain sahab', आप.
MUMMY: 'Bhabhi ji' | 'भाभी जी', आप. She says 'Captain sahab', आप.
PAPA: 'Bhai sahab' | 'भाई साहब', आप. Papa says 'Captain sahab', आप.
MAMA JI: no name, तुम since the dropped catch; his greeting is 'Catch?' Mama ji says 'Captain sahab', आप.
MAUSI: 'Madam ji' | 'मैडम जी', as her old pupils call her, आप.
MAUSA JI: 'Lineman sahab' | 'लाइनमैन साहब', आप. Mausa ji says 'Captain sahab', आप.
MASTERJI: 'Master' | 'मास्टर', आप; Masterji calls him 'Captain', आप. They argue in आप.
A CHILD OR A LANE PLAYER: 'khiladi' | 'खिलाड़ी', तुम; first names in his life, but never a card person's name or note word in a bubble before or during a decision (rule 36).
All of these go into the cast map's one address table, checked by the Hindi-first readers and the South Indian reader (rule 65).

SORRY AT THE GROUND (once a chapter; he gave a lane player out, then saw the ball had hit the bat, and takes it back at once in front of both lanes, as no one did for him): EN 'Not out. I slipped up, player.' | HINGLISH 'Not out. Mujhse chook hui, khiladi.' | HINDI 'नॉट आउट। मुझसे चूक हुई, खिलाड़ी।'

SORRY (to Mummy, who said the floodlight bulbs were fine and was right; plain): EN 'I slipped up, Bhabhi ji. The bulbs were fine.' | HINGLISH 'Mujhse chook ho gayi, Bhabhi ji. Bulb theek the.' | HINDI 'मुझसे चूक हो गई, भाभी जी। बल्ब ठीक थे।'

COMFORTING (Mummy, the morning after the flood; kept; his one coded comfort of the chapter): EN 'Next ball, Bhabhi ji. The shutter goes up tomorrow too.' | HINGLISH 'Next ball, Bhabhi ji. Shutter kal bhi uthega.' | HINDI 'अगली गेंद, भाभी जी। शटर कल भी उठेगा।'

COMFORTING A LANE PLAYER (out cheaply, walking back; plain): EN 'Never mind, player. The best of them get out.' | HINGLISH 'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Achhe-achhe out hote hain.' | HINDI 'कोई बात नहीं, खिलाड़ी। अच्छे-अच्छे आउट होते हैं।'

LOSING HIS TEMPER (a scooter on the pitch; a whisper bubble, the finger up, then a second bubble after a long beat): EN 'Wait. Whose scooter is this? / Off my pitch.' | HINGLISH 'Ruko. Kiska scooter hai? / Meri pitch se hatao.' | HINDI 'रुको। किसका स्कूटर है? / मेरी पिच से हटाओ।'
A JOKE (about his knee; kept): EN 'Retired hurt. Just the knee.' | HINGLISH 'Retired hurt. Sirf ghutna.' | HINDI 'घुटना छुट्टी पर। मैं नहीं।'

A JOKE ABOUT HIS AGE (to Tinku, who asks why he no longer bowls; depot words): EN 'Old model, Scorer. No spare parts.' | HINGLISH 'Purana model hoon, Scorer. Parts nahin milte.' | HINDI 'पुराना मॉडल हूँ, स्कोरर। पार्ट्स नहीं मिलते।'
THE GRUDGE (any talk of umpires, luck or fairness): EN 'One trial. Not out. Ask anyone.' | HINGLISH 'Ek hi trial tha. Not out. Kisi se poochh lo.' | HINDI 'एक ही ट्रायल था। नॉट आउट। किसी से पूछ लो।'
ASKING AFTER NANI (to Papa, every morning on the walk from May; one word, and Papa answers with a time): EN 'Nani ji?' | HINGLISH 'Nani ji?' | HINDI 'नानी जी?'
HIS TURN (4.26, at dusk, on the page, to Tinku; kept word for word): EN 'That book. Show the district.' | HINGLISH 'Wo kitaab. Zile ko dikhao.' | HINDI 'वो किताब। ज़िले को दिखाओ।'
THE STORY'S FIXED ENDING (4.27, off panel, the same in every band; kept): EN 'Over. Both lanes mended it.' | HINGLISH 'Over. Dono galiyon ne milkar banayi.' | HINDI 'ओवर। दोनों गलियों ने मिलकर बनाई।'

habits: The phone: a plain phone in a plain dark case with a cracked top corner, kept in a trouser pocket. Painted with a blank screen; every message is live text on it, or a message card under the panel if the phone is small (rules 30 and 40). No app name, app look or 'forwarded' label (rule 3), and no quirk about his eyes or the font size.

Script: English in Latin letters only, never Devanagari and never a Hinglish sentence (realism notes 2.3). The messages are strings of nouns and calls, not English clauses, so this does not break his speech's no-clause rule.
Shape: a telegram in his speaking shape, the thing first, then the place, then one instruction, 1 to 7 words.
His typed yes is 'Not out', his not-yet 'Wait', his enough 'Over'; the lane knows a message is his by it. When he thanks, he types it plainly: 'thank you'.
Figures: none, except the cup's date and its nine o'clock, as digits and only in cup messages. Never a minute, never a score, never a price.

Punctuation: none at all, not even a question mark. The phone capitalises the first letter, and that is his only capital. Never all capitals, which reads as shouting and is the 'WhatsApp uncle' trap (realism notes 7).
The one exception: once a year, in his own family group (mentioned, never shown), he writes the cup's end in full sentences with full stops. That is the tell that it matters.
Emoji: one only, 🏏, on cup messages. Tinku's 🏏 to him copies his. No faces, no folded hands, no stickers, no good-morning flowers, no forwards, ever.
Voice notes: never sends one. He listens to the first few seconds of anyone else's and answers with the one fact asked, or a call.

He sends the same words one by one to every person rather than to a group: he trusts a message he has sent himself. The lane's group exists and is mentioned, never shown (owner, 23 Oct: no group chat).
Reads and answers twice a day, after the walk and before the toss, and within a minute about cricket or the drain; never late at night (he walks at dawn).
One forefinger, slow and deliberate; no typos, because there are so few words.
samples: TO THE WHOLE LANE, one number at a time, the same words to each (kept): 'Cup 15 aug ground 9 am 🏏' (the cup's date and its nine, his only typed figures)
TO MAUSI, after her two-minute voice note about when to send the lane side's lunch (kept from the cast map): '9 am'
TO PAPA, the May morning Papa is on the night train (he has walked their route alone): 'Route clear'
TO TINKU, the night before the cup (the chair in the shade is his tenderness): 'Scorer chair in shade bring book'
TO MUMMY, when she texts that the floodlight bulbs are put aside: 'Not out' (his typed yes; next morning the full price is on her counter)
TO MAUSA JI, the night the rewired floodlights first come on (plain thanks): 'Lights on thank you lineman sahab'
TO MASTERJI, the morning after the July flood: 'Drain cracked your side' (Masterji's reply, not his: 'aapki side')
TO MAMA JI, when the trophy is promised again: 'Catch' (his greeting, typed with no question mark)
TO YOU, on your birthday (kept): 'Happy birthday front foot'
TO HIS OWN FAMILY GROUP (mentioned, never shown; his one message a year in full sentences; the same in every band): 'The cup is over. Both lanes mended the drain together. 🏏'

test_lines.moment: 1. The lights go out in the middle of dinner (to the table, Nani among them, so 'Rukiye', then to Mausa ji; no exclamation, since 'Arre waah' is only for good cricket; dry humour).
test_lines.en: Hold on. Lineman sahab, you're in.

test_lines.moment: 2. Someone everyone was waiting for arrives two hours late (to Mama ji at the gate; a whisper bubble, the verdict finger up and kept up, no figure; plain Hindi, the old catch as the reason).
test_lines.en: Now? That's how the catch went too.
test_lines.hinglish: Ab aaye? Catch bhi aise hi chhoota tha.
test_lines.hi: अब आए? कैच भी ऐसे ही छूटा था।

test_lines.moment: 3. A cousin phones to say they have got their first job (to the cousin on the phone; his once-a-year praise, then an infinitive command, so the cousin keeps no gender).
test_lines.en: Well played. Now stay at the crease.
test_lines.hinglish: Well played. Ab tik ke khelna.
test_lines.hi: बढ़िया पारी। अब टिक के खेलना।

test_lines.moment: 4. The tea someone has just made has far too much sugar in it (to Masterji, who made it; a polite no, the reason from the depot).
test_lines.en: Too sweet, Master. Like the depot canteen's.
test_lines.hinglish: Zyada meethi hai, Master. Bilkul depot canteen wali.
test_lines.hi: ज़्यादा मीठी है, मास्टर। बिल्कुल डिपो कैंटीन वाली।

test_lines.moment: 5. In front of the family, he is shown to have had a fact wrong (to Papa, who has shown that the station clock runs slow; his plain sorry, said at once).
test_lines.en: I slipped up, Bhai sahab. The clock is slow.
test_lines.hinglish: Mujhse chook ho gayi, Bhai sahab. Ghadi dheemi hai.
test_lines.hi: मुझसे चूक हो गई, भाई साहब। घड़ी धीमी है।

test_lines.moment: 6. Someone he loves is leaving, goodbye on a railway platform (to you; his hello, then a command, rule 66 clear).
test_lines.en: Front foot. Be back for the cup.
test_lines.hinglish: Front foot. Cup pe zaroor aao.
test_lines.hi: फ़्रंट फ़ुट। कप पे ज़रूर आओ।

test_lines.moment: 7. Someone thanks him for something he did (Tinku, for his chair in the shade every cup; 'Kis baat ka?' and the credit sent elsewhere, which keeps his 4.26 turn unspent).
test_lines.en: What for, Scorer? The shade's for the book.
test_lines.hinglish: Kis baat ka, Scorer? Chhaon kitaab ke liye hai.
test_lines.hi: किस बात का, स्कोरर? छाँव किताब के लिए है।

test_lines.moment: 8. A neighbour passes on a rumour that the corner sweet shop is closing (to Mummy, who heard it at her counter; an appeal turned down with what he saw on his dawn walk; a habit of judging, never a character).
test_lines.en: Not out, Bhabhi ji. Their stove was lit at dawn.
test_lines.hinglish: Not out, Bhabhi ji. Subah bhatti jal rahi thi.
test_lines.hi: नॉट आउट, भाभी जी। सुबह भट्टी जल रही थी।

test_lines.moment: 9. Heavy rain floods the lane outside the house (to the lane, you among them; worry as an order, then the depot; verbless order, rule 66 clear).
test_lines.en: Off the drain. I've got the depot tarpaulin.
test_lines.hinglish: Naali se door. Depot ka tirpal hai mere paas.
test_lines.hi: नाली से दूर। डिपो का तिरपाल है मेरे पास।

test_lines.moment: 10. Someone asks him how he is (you ask; a plain answer, then his knee in depot words; no figure, no dodge).
test_lines.en: I'm fine. Just the knee, in for servicing.
test_lines.hinglish: Theek hoon. Bas ghutna servicing mein.
test_lines.hi: ठीक हूँ। बस घुटना सर्विसिंग में।

test_lines.moment: 11. A child knocks a glass of water across the table (to the child, a grandchild at the table; plain comfort; 'khiladi' fits any child).
test_lines.hinglish: Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.
test_lines.hi: कोई बात नहीं, खिलाड़ी। होता है।

test_lines.moment: 12. A phone call brings good news (to the caller; his exclamation, quiet).
test_lines.en: Arre waah. Right off the middle of the bat.
test_lines.hinglish: Arre waah. Bilkul bat ke beech se.
test_lines.hi: अरे वाह। बिल्कुल बैट के बीच से।

changed: KEPT: who he is. Essence, want, fear and contradiction (strict by the book, still sore about one trial), the turn at 4.26 ('That book. Show the district.'), the stakes at 4.03, the fixed ending at 4.27, the toss as his word alone, the still, whispering anger, and every line the readers marked as ringing true: 'Straight bat. Front foot.' as his hello, 'Arre waah' said quietly at a clean catch, 'Retired hurt. Sirf ghutna.', 'Nau matlab nau, Bhai sahab.', 'Next ball, Bhabhi ji. Shutter kal bhi uthega.', 'Lineman sahab, aapki batting.', 'khiladi' for any child, 'Madam ji', 'Lineman sahab', and the texts 'Happy birthday front foot' and 'Cup 15 aug ground 9 am 🏏'.

THE CARICATURE (real-India note): a call opened 10 of his 12 test lines and every feeling was an umpire's word. Now the shape is two beats, verdict then one reason, and the verdict is a call only at the ground or on a ruling; at the gate it is plain lane Hindi with a depot reason. Calls now sit in 3 of his 12 test lines ('Well played', 'Front foot', 'Not out'; three more carry a cricket picture: 'aapki batting', the old catch, 'bat ke beech se') and in under half his sample bubbles.

FEELINGS IN PLAIN WORDS (cast-wide 3): sorry is 'Mujhse chook ho gayi, Bhai sahab. Ghadi dheemi hai.' (was 'Dead ball. Umpire ki chook. Next ball.'); thanks is 'Badi meherbani, Lineman sahab.' and, with the deed, 'Poore paise, Bhabhi ji. Aaj mol-bhaav nahin.' (was 'Well fielded' to both); when thanked, 'Kis baat ka, Scorer?' (was 'Over, Scorer.'); comfort is 'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.'; love also comes as the bat he kept for you ('Tumhara purana bat hai mere paas. / Nayi grip ke saath.'); his fear is said plainly to Papa ('Scooter badh rahe hain, Bhai sahab. / Mere baad, ye parking.', was 'Last over, Bhai sahab. Maidan pe scooter.'). Each cricket code for a feeling now comes at most once a chapter, beside its plain form.

THE READERS' LINES, used as given: moment 2 'Ab aaye? Catch bhi aise hi chhoota tha.' (was 'Timed out. Catch ki tarah.'); moment 11 'Koi baat nahin, khiladi. Hota hai.' (was 'Catch chhoota. Hota hai, khiladi. Next ball.'); the grudge 'Ek hi trial tha. Not out. Kisi se poochh lo.' (was 'Mera iklauta trial ...', since 'iklauta' is said of an only child).
POLITENESS (Hindi rules note a): moment 1 opens 'Rukiye.' | 'रुकिए।', since Nani, who is older than him, is at the table. 'Ruko' now goes only to players and anyone younger.

RULE 22 (Hindi rules note b, cast-wide 5, real-India note): 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin.' leaves the test set and his stock replies. It stays only for a harmless rumour, fenced in his never list with every proof word, never in a chapter or beat that holds a report of harassment or a dowry demand. Moment 8 is now a ruling backed by what he saw: 'Not out, Bhabhi ji. Subah bhatti jal rahi thi.'

HINDI MODE (Hindi rules note, real-India note, cast-wide 11): no English cricket phrase in Devanagari that Sunita and Meena could not read. नेक्स्ट बॉल becomes अगली गेंद, वेल प्लेड बढ़िया पारी, वेल फ़ील्डेड अच्छा पकड़ा (बढ़िया फ़ील्डिंग off the field), क्लीन कैच साफ़ कैच, डेड बॉल ये गेंद नहीं गिनी जाएगी, रिटायर्ड हर्ट घुटना छुट्टी पर ('घुटना छुट्टी पर। मैं नहीं।' for the knee joke). आउट, नॉट आउट, नो बॉल, कैच, फ़्रंट फ़ुट and सीधा बैट stay. 'Timed out' leaves his voice in every mode, since the readers found it obscure even in English; the Hindi rules note's 'टाइम आउट। उस कैच की तरह।' is not needed, because moment 2 no longer uses it. Hinglish keeps the English calls.

COMMON FILLERS ARE FREE (cast-wide 1): the bans on arre, achha, chalo, suno, dekho, bas, theek and haan are gone; he says 'Achha, Scorer, ...' and 'Bas ghutna ...' mid-line. 'Arre' is no longer his alone; he keeps the phrase 'Arre waah' said quietly. His never list now names other people's phrases and shapes only.
ENGLISH VERB WITH KAR (cast-wide 2): allowed where it suits him, for a machine job, the depot's way ('Grip change karo. Depot ka tube lagao.'). His knee stays 'Retired hurt', the rang-true call.
URDU-ROOTED WORDS (cast-wide 8): 'meherbani', 'zaroor' and 'waqt' are in his everyday Hindi ('Badi meherbani', 'Cup pe zaroor aao'), so they belong to the town, not to Masterji.
MORE VERBS (cast-wide 9): plain lines now carry their 'hai', 'tha' or 'hoon' ('Bat laga tha.', 'Theek hoon.', 'Purana model hoon, Scorer.'); bare shapes stay for calls and orders.

ENGLISH MODE (real-India note, cast-wide 10): 'Oh, nice.' goes; 'Arre waah.' stays in English as Mami's 'Ish' does, with 'Shot.' as the readers' fallback, only at a stroke. 'It took the bat' becomes 'It hit the bat'; 'Much obliged' and 'I slipped up' give him an older Englishman's plain words.

NO COINED SAYINGS: he has no proverbs. 'Achhe-achhe out hote hain' is everyday Hindi and was chosen over 'bade-bade', which brings a famous film line to mind. 'Saboot nahin, toh ungli nahin' is his own ruling on the real idiom 'ungli uthana', not a saying.

CLASHES AVOIDED with the other rewrites: 'Shabaash' stays Mausi's, 'Aap sahi hain' and 'Theek hai, maan liya' stay Masterji's, 'Isme kya' stays with Mama ji, Mummy and Mausa ji. One shared opening is left on purpose because the readers wrote it: 'Koi baat nahin' in moment 11, which Mummy, Papa and Mausi also say; 'khiladi' and 'Hota hai' mark his.
TYPING: unchanged in shape. One new plain thanks, 'Lights on thank you lineman sahab' to Mausa ji; the rule against typing 'ok' is no longer pinned on other people.

KNOCK-ON FOR HIS CAST FILE AND OTHERS: never_does 'Says sorry in words.' must go (he now does, plainly, except to the trial's umpire and to Nani); his MUMMY relationship ('Not out, Bhabhi ji. Next ball.' becomes 'Next ball, Bhabhi ji. Shutter kal bhi uthega.', and his thanks becomes 'Poore paise'); his MAUSA JI relationship (thanks is 'Badi meherbani'); his essence's 'answers most questions with an umpire's call' becomes 'at the ground'; matrix 2.14 and 2.15 rows for him ('Next ball' sorry, 'Well fielded' thanks, sole owner of 'arre').

FOR THE READERS (rule 65): Hindi-first readers check 'मुझसे चूक हो गई' as an everyday sorry (fallback 'ग़लती मेरी'), 'बड़ी मेहरबानी', 'घुटना छुट्टी पर। मैं नहीं।', 'अच्छा पकड़ा' for a fielding stop, 'अच्छे-अच्छे आउट होते हैं', and 'टिक के खेलना'; English-mode readers check 'Arre waah' left in English and 'player' for 'khiladi'. The checker run on this file is clean apart from moment 1, said to a table: its rule 66 flag on 'Rukiye' | 'रुकिए' is a polite form that shows no gender, and its address flag on 'sahab' | 'साहब' is Mausa ji's title, not a word for you.
